newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE agrees to disagree on Albania force.
newsitem.headline: OSCE agrees to disagree on Albania force.

text.p: Members of Europe's top security body reached broad agreement on Wednesday to send a humanitarian mission to Albania but failed to find common ground on a foreign protection force, officials said.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) permanent council broke up without finding a consensus on the wording of an endorsement to legitimise an international military presence in the strife-torn Balkan state.
"We have a problem in that we do not have a precedent and we cannot immediately overcome this," permanent council chairman Lars Vissing told a news conference after the talks.
"But no particular states questioned the action to protect services so I am confident we will have an early success."

He planned to continue informal talks with several nations starting on Thursday and call a fresh meeting of the permanent council when he had the basis for a consensus. The 54-member OSCE groups most of Europe, the United States and Canada.

"The differences with previous situations are very real. Past interventions were by United Nations mandated troops. Albania is appealing to have foreign troops to protect aid deliveries. That is very new, very original," Vissing said.

Diplomatic sources said Russia in particular had raised concerns about backing the deployment of foreign military. Some OSCE nations felt the United Nations was better placed to give a mandate for a multinational force, they added.
"The sticking point was the United Nations mandate," a Western diplomat told reporters.
Vissing said the OSCE was working towards a text that would allow the organisation to express its endorsement of operations conducted by the so-called "coalition of the willing".

Several European countries, including Italy, Spain, Greece, and France have said they are prepared to send forces to ensure aid convoys reach their destinations and provide protection to civilian operations.
The chairman said the OSCE permanent council had made substantial progress, however, in the wording of a second document dealing with a humanitarian mission but he declined to reveal details.
"The civilian part is what the OSCE normally does -- safeguarding democracy, preparing elections, monitoring elections," he said.
"No one is dissatisfied with the wording of the draft proposal for civilian operations...This is today's achievement."

A 15-strong European team, including European Union and OSCE representatives, was visting Albania on Wednesday to assess the situation. Diplomatic sources said the framework for the OSCE's humanitarian mission would become clearer once the team reported its findings.
"I would envisage 25 or more people in Tirana then additional local coverage in field offices to help local administrations get going," Vissing said.
He forecast an OSCE presence would remain in the chaos-ridden country at least until early general elections, planned by June.
Former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky had agreed to stay on as the OSCE's representative to Albania, Austria's ambassador to the OSCE Jutta Stefan-Bastl told reporters.
